newsitem.title: VIETNAM: Laotian describes firing squad ordeal in Vietnam.
newsitem.headline: Laotian describes firing squad ordeal in Vietnam.

text.p: A Laotian drugs-trafficker who cheated death just moments before he was to be executed by a Vietnamese firing squad has described his ordeal and vowed never to get involved in narcotics again.

Sieng Pheng said in an interview, published on Wednesday, that his ears had buzzed and his body had been gripped by fear as he was led into a room beside the execution grounds where his last words were to be recorded.

"At that time I was too scared, I was sweating, my ears were filled with noise," he told the An Ninh Thu Do newspaper. "At that point I asked to declare further information, so that if I died I would have a clean conscience, but also I hoped the officials would be lenient."
Sieng Pheng was arrested in 1995 after he was caught trying to smuggle 15 kg (33 pounds) of heroin by car to Hanoi from the Laotian border.
He was sentenced to death, but managed to win a last minute reprieve by offering to reveal new information on a network of accomplices as an execution squad was readying to kill him.
The information he provided led directly to the uncovering of a major syndicate involving several members of Vietnam's feared and respected security establishment.

In May this year the case came to trial. Eight people, including police and border guards, were sentenced to death and others given lengthy jail terms. Huge crowds gathered outside the Hanoi court building as the sentencing was delivered.
Investigations are still continuing and a trial involving some of the 40 other people who've been arrested in connection with the case is expected later this year.
Vietnam was due to announce formally on Wednesday that the death sentence against Sieng Pheng had been commuted to life imprisonment as the result of a rare presidential pardon.

"This shows the leniency of the state and people towards those who commit crimes, but later repent, giving honest declarations about themselves and their accomplices, and redeeming themselves for their faults," an official at the presidential office said by telephone.
Sieng Pheng, who learned of the news on Monday, said he would never return to drugs and added that he wanted to thank the Vietnamese state and officials for sparing his life.
"I was so scared," he said. "I promise I will be well re-educated in prison so I can soon be released from jail to see my wife and children and my parents."

Vietnam, with its lengthy land and sea borders, has become both a market and conduit for illegal narcotics from the notorious Golden Triangle producing region which straddles the borders of Burma, China, Thailand and Laos.

The trial in May was the biggest-yet of its kind in Vietnam and highlighted the problem while also pitting the rule of law against the power and influence of individuals in a security establishment once seen as being virtually untouchable.
